title: Magnets: The Invisible Pull
summary: How magnets attract iron and steel, how their poles attract and repel, how Earth's magnetic field guides a compass, and how people use lodestone and electromagnets.
poll: Magnets are more useful to people today than they were long ago.

versions.title: The Pull You Can Not See
versions.text:
Hold a magnet near a pin. Zip! The pin jumps to it. A magnet can pull on some things. We say it can attract them. But you can not see the pull.

A magnet pulls things made of iron. It pulls steel, too. It will not pull wood or glass.

Each magnet has two ends. Each end is a pole. One is north. One is south.

Put two like poles close. They push off. They repel. Put north by south. They snap close. They attract.

The pull fills the space by a magnet. It is strong up close. It is weak far off. It can pull through thin paper.

Our Earth acts like a huge magnet. A compass has a small magnet in it. It points north. It helps us find the way. Long ago, men on ships used one. Men on camels in the sand did, too.

Long ago, men found a rock that could pull iron. It was lodestone. It was the first magnet.

Some magnets work with power from a wire. Turn the power on. They pull. Turn it off. They let go. Big ones can lift old cars!

versions.title: Magnets: The Invisible Pull
versions.text:
Hold a magnet close to a pin, and the pin leaps across the gap and sticks to it. Nothing seems to touch the pin, yet it moves. A magnet can attract certain objects without touching them. This pull is a force, but it is invisible.

Magnets attract objects made of iron. They also attract steel, because steel contains iron. A magnet will not pull on wood, glass, paper, or most plastic.

Every magnet has two ends called poles. One is the north pole, and the other is the south pole. If you push two north poles together, they push each other apart. Scientists say that like poles repel. But if you bring a north pole near a south pole, they snap together. Opposite poles attract.

The space around a magnet where its force can be felt is called its magnetic field. The field is strongest near the poles. It gets weaker as you move farther away. The force can even pass through a thin sheet of paper.

Our whole planet acts like one giant magnet with its own field. A compass has a tiny magnet inside, called a needle, that always points north. For hundreds of years, sailors used a compass to guide their ships. Travelers crossing the Arabian desert on camels used one, too.

Long ago, people discovered a special rock that could pull on iron. It was called lodestone. It was the first magnet that people knew about.

Some magnets are made with electricity. An electromagnet works only when electric power flows through its wire. When the power is on, it pulls. When the power is off, it lets go. Large electromagnets can lift old cars!

versions.text:
Hold a magnet near a metal pin, and the pin leaps across the gap and clings to it, even though nothing visible connects the two objects. This mysterious behavior occurs because a magnet generates an invisible force that is capable of attracting particular materials across empty space without physically contacting them at all, a property that has fascinated philosophers, inventors, and ordinary curious observers for thousands upon thousands of years.

Magnets attract objects containing iron, including steel, which itself consists predominantly of iron combined with other elements. Nevertheless, a magnet will not exert any detectable attraction whatsoever on wood, glass, paper, or most common varieties of plastic, regardless of how very powerful the particular magnet happens to be.

Every magnet possesses two distinct extremities called poles, which scientists designate precisely as the north pole and the south pole. When two north poles are pushed deliberately toward each other, they forcefully shove one another apart. This is precisely why physicists consistently explain that like poles repel one another. When a north pole approaches a south pole, by contrast, the two snap together immediately and firmly, because opposite poles reliably attract.

The region surrounding any magnet in which its invisible force can actually be detected is called its magnetic field. This field is consistently most intense near the poles themselves. It weakens greatly as the measured distance from the magnet increases, although this invisible influence can nonetheless still penetrate a thin sheet of ordinary paper without any apparent difficulty whatsoever.

Our entire planet behaves remarkably like one gigantic magnet enveloped continuously by its own substantial magnetic field. A simple compass contains a tiny magnetized needle that consistently aligns itself with that planetary field in order to indicate geographic north reliably. For hundreds upon hundreds of years, sailors depended heavily on compasses to navigate their vessels successfully across the otherwise featureless ocean. Travelers traversing the vast Arabian desert on camels relied on them equally, particularly whenever clouds or sandstorms concealed the familiar constellations that ordinarily guided them through the night.

Centuries ago, people first discovered an unusual natural mineral that could spontaneously attract iron on its own. It was called lodestone, and it was the earliest magnet that human beings ever recognized and eventually learned to utilize for genuinely practical purposes, including the construction of the very first primitive compasses used in navigation.

Some magnets, by contrast, are generated entirely artificially through the application of electricity rather than occurring naturally. An electromagnet operates exclusively while an electric current actively circulates through its tightly coiled wire. When the current is deliberately activated, the electromagnet pulls strongly; when the current is subsequently interrupted, it immediately releases whatever object it was holding. Industrial electromagnets installed in recycling facilities are sufficiently powerful to elevate entire abandoned automobiles and deposit them precisely wherever their human operators require, a task that would be genuinely impossible using ordinary natural magnets of comparable size.

versions.title: Magnetism: The Invisible Force
versions.text:
Hold a magnet near a metal pin, and the pin leaps across the intervening gap and clings to it firmly, even though nothing visible connects the two objects whatsoever. This mysterious behavior occurs because a magnet generates an invisible force field that is capable of attracting particular materials across empty space without ever physically contacting them at all, a remarkable property that has fascinated philosophers, inventors, and ordinary curious observers alike for thousands upon thousands of years throughout recorded human history.

Magnets attract objects containing iron, including steel, which itself consists predominantly of iron combined deliberately with other alloying elements. Nevertheless, a magnet will not exert any detectable attraction whatsoever on wood, glass, paper, or most common varieties of plastic, regardless of how extraordinarily powerful the particular magnet in question happens to be constructed.

Every magnet possesses two distinct physical extremities called poles, which scientists designate precisely and consistently as the north pole and the south pole. When two north poles are pushed deliberately toward one another, they forcefully shove each other apart with considerable resistance, which is precisely why physicists consistently explain that like poles repel one another; when a north pole instead approaches a south pole, by stark contrast, the two snap together immediately and quite firmly, because opposite poles reliably and predictably attract one another.

The surrounding region around any given magnet in which its invisible force can actually be measured and detected is called its magnetic field. This field is consistently most intense in the immediate vicinity of the poles themselves, and it weakens considerably and predictably as the measured distance from the magnet steadily increases, although this invisible influence can nonetheless still readily penetrate a thin sheet of ordinary paper without any apparent difficulty whatsoever, demonstrating its genuinely pervasive nature.

Our entire planet behaves remarkably like one single, gigantic magnet enveloped continuously by its own substantial, planet-spanning magnetic field. A simple handheld compass contains a tiny magnetized needle that consistently aligns itself with that enormous planetary field in order to indicate geographic north with impressive reliability. For hundreds upon hundreds of years spanning numerous civilizations, sailors depended heavily on compasses to navigate their vessels successfully across the otherwise featureless and disorienting open ocean, and travelers traversing the vast Arabian desert on camels relied upon them equally heavily, particularly whenever thick clouds or sudden sandstorms concealed the familiar constellations that would otherwise have guided them safely through the night.

Centuries ago, people first discovered by chance an unusual natural mineral that could spontaneously attract iron entirely on its own, without any human intervention whatsoever. It was called lodestone, and it represented the earliest magnet that human beings ever recognized and subsequently learned to utilize for genuinely practical purposes of many kinds, including, crucially, the construction of the very first primitive compasses ever used for maritime and overland navigation.

Some magnets, by deliberate contrast, are generated entirely artificially through the controlled application of electricity rather than occurring naturally within the earth. An electromagnet operates exclusively and only while an electric current actively circulates through its tightly wound coiled wire. When the current is deliberately activated by an operator, the electromagnet pulls with considerable force; when the current is subsequently interrupted or switched off, it immediately releases whatever object it had been holding without delay. Industrial electromagnets installed within modern recycling facilities are sufficiently powerful to elevate entire abandoned automobiles effortlessly and deposit them precisely wherever their human operators require, a remarkable task that would be genuinely impossible to accomplish using ordinary natural magnets of any comparable physical size.

MID.prompt: Explain the difference between an ordinary magnet and an electromagnet. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I described both kinds of magnets.
I explained what switching the power on and off does.
I used at least two details from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: An ordinary magnet and an electromagnet both create a magnetic field that can attract or repel certain metal objects, but they work in different ways. An ordinary magnet, like lodestone, always has this pulling force whether or not anyone is using it. An electromagnet, however, is made with electricity flowing through a coiled wire, so it only has a magnetic field while the power is switched on. Switching the power off lets go of whatever the electromagnet was holding, which is very useful, because powerful electromagnets can lift heavy objects like old cars and then release them exactly when needed.

HIGH.prompt: Magnetism is invisible, yet people have relied on it for centuries. Explain how two different uses of magnets in the article depend on the rules of magnetism.
checklist: I described two uses of magnets from the article.
I connected each use to a rule of magnetism (poles, fields, or current).
I used precise evidence from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Magnetism is invisible, yet two very different uses described in the article both depend on its basic rules. The compass, which people have used for centuries to navigate deserts and seas, works because a tiny needle made from a magnetic material, much like the ancient lodestone, aligns itself with the planet's own magnetic field, always settling toward north. In contrast, an electromagnet depends on the rule that electric current flowing through a coiled wire creates a magnetic field of its own, meaning the pull exists only while the current flows and vanishes the instant the power is switched off. Although a compass relies on a field that is always present and an electromagnet relies on a field that can be turned on and off, both inventions prove how precisely people have learned to harness an invisible force they cannot even see.
